"## Best practices for preserving named entities, terminology, and numbers in localized output: guidance from localization industry bodies (GALA, TAUS, CSA Research, ISO 17100) # Preserving Named Entities, Terminology, and Numbers in Localization: Guidance from Industry Bodies **Scope note:** Findings below summarize the published guidance and standards of the four requested bodies as of my last knowledge update. GALA, TAUS, and CSA Research publish much of this via member content, blogs, and paywalled reports, so verify exact titles/editions against current sources; ISO 17100 is the only auditable formal standard among them. --- ## 1. ISO 17100:2015 — Translation Services Requirements [1] The standard is process-based rather than prescriptive about specific entities/numbers, but it mandates the mechanisms that protect them: - **Pre-production agreement:** The translation service provider (TSP) must agree with the client on project specifications including **terminology/glossaries, style guides, and reference materials** before work begins; client-supplied termbases must be used and gaps flagged. - **Source-content query obligation:** Errors or ambiguities in the source (inconsistent names, unclear numbers, contradictory terminology) must be **recorded and queried to the client**, not silently "corrected." - **Two-person workflow:** Every translation requires a **"check" by a second qualified linguist**, explicitly covering accuracy, completeness, and **terminology consistency** — the main audit hook for altered names, mistranscribed numbers, and non-approved terms. - **Competence requirements:** Translators/revisers must demonstrate **research and information-acquisition ability**, underpinning verification of proper nouns and domain terms. **Related standards:** ISO 18587:2017 (post-editing of MT) treats **named entities, numbers, dates, and terminology** as classic MT failure points that post-editors must verify even under light post-editing [2]; ISO 26162 governs termbase management, and ISO 704/1087 govern terminology-work principles [3]. ## 2. GALA — Globalization and Localization Association [4] GALA's educational content centers on **linguistic asset management** as the preservation mechanism: - Build and maintain **termbases** with approved, banned, and conditional terms (definitions, part of speech, context, status), validated with client SMEs before kickoff. - Maintain **"Do Not Translate" (DNT) lists** for brand names, product names, trademarks, UI strings, and code identifiers; decide per locale whether proper nouns are kept in source script or transliterated, and record the decision. - Enforce **locale conventions** for numbers, dates, currencies, units, addresses, and phone formats — typically referencing **Unicode CLDR** as the formatting authority [8]. - Run **automated QA** (terminology consistency, number matching, untranslatable protection) as a standard workflow gate. ## 3. TAUS — Dynamic Quality Framework (DQF) [5] TAUS contributes the **measurement layer** — error typologies that make preservation failures countable: - The TAUS DQF error typology includes explicit categories for **terminology** (non-use of approved terms), **accuracy errors** (mistranslation, additions, omissions — where corrupted numbers and names surface), and **locale-convention errors** (wrong number/date/currency formats) and company-style errors. - TAUS guidance on MT evaluation stresses that **entity and number corruption is a high-severity, meaning-changing error class**, best caught via automated checks (regex/number comparison, DNT string matching) in MT and post-editing pipelines. ## 4. CSA Research [6] CSA Research provides the **business case and maturity framing**: - Enterprises at higher stages of CSA's **Localization Maturity Model (LMM)** maintain central termbases and style guides; terminology management is positioned as ROI-positive (less rework, fewer review cycles, brand consistency). - **Brand/product naming guidance:** define which names are protected (never translated), test names per market for negative connotations and trademark conflicts, and centralize naming decisions so all vendors apply identical treatment. - **Global-readiness checks:** validate number, currency, date, and address formatting per locale pre-launch; treat numeric format/value errors as release blockers. ## 5. Cross-cutting: MQM as the shared taxonomy [7] The **Multidimensional Quality Metrics (MQM)** typology — developed in the QTLaunchPad project and widely adopted across the industry (and used in CSA/TAUS-adjacent quality work) — makes preservation auditable via explicit issue types: *Terminology*, *Mistranslation*, *Addition/Omission*, and *Locale convention* (numbers, dates, formats). --- ## Consolidated Best Practices (synthesis of the above) | Area | Practice | Source basis | |---|---|---| | **Named entities** | Inventory entity classes; decide keep/transliterate/translate per locale; store as DNT or termbase entries; verify against authoritative sources; auto-check DNT strings | [1][4][6] | | **Terminology** | Client-approved termbase before kickoff; enforce via CAT + automated QA; non-use of approved terms = reportable error; change-controlled updates | [1][3][4][5][6] | | **Numbers** | Adapt *format* to locale (separators, currency, units, dates — per CLDR) but never alter *values*; automated source/target number comparison; verify in post-editing | [2][4][5][8] | | **Process** | Query source ambiguities rather than guessing; second-linguist check; QA gates; version-controlled linguistic assets with feedback loops | [1][4][6] | --- ## Sources [1] ISO 17100:2015, *Translation services — Requirements for translation services* [2] ISO 18587:2017, *Post-editing of machine translation output* [3] ISO 26162 (term bases); ISO 704 & ISO 1087 (terminology work) [4] GALA knowledge base / published articles on linguistic assets, terminology management, DNT lists, and locale formatting [5] TAUS Dynamic Quality Framework (DQF) error typology and MT quality evaluation guidance [6] CSA Research reports on terminology management, the Localization Maturity Model, global brand naming, and global readiness [7] MQM — Multidimensional Quality Metrics (QTLaunchPad/industry adoption) [8] Unicode CLDR (locale data: numbers, dates, currencies) --- ## How machine translation systems handle named entities and numbers: NER-based protection, do-not-translate lists, copy-source rules, and MQM error typology categories for entity/number mistranslation I'll research this topic systematically, starting with how MT systems protect named entities and numbers. --- ## Inline markup and tag handling in localization: XLIFF inline tags, placeholder and variable protection in CAT tools, ICU MessageFormat, W3C Internationalization Tag Set (ITS) # Inline Markup & Tag Handling in Localization — Findings ## 1. XLIFF inline tags **XLIFF 1.2 (OASIS Standard, Feb 2008) [1]** — five inline elements embedded directly in ``/``: - `` / `` — begin/end of a paired native code (e.g., `…`); paired via `rid` or matching `id` - `` — standalone placeholder code (e.g., `
`, `{0}`) - `` — isolated begin/end code (`pos="open|close"`) - `` — translatable content nested inside a code - Key attributes: `ctype` (code type, e.g., `bold`, `italic`), `equiv-text` (human-readable display hint); the native code itself is stored as (escaped) element content. **XLIFF 2.x (2.0 in 2014; 2.1 in 2019; 2.2 in 2020) [2][3][10]** — completely redesigned inline model: - Elements: ``, `` (paired code containing content), ``/`` (start/end codes, may be unpaired or overlapping), ``/`` (spanning annotation markers) - Original native codes are stored out-of-line in `/` and referenced with `dataRef`, keeping source/target clean; `disp` (display text) and `equiv` (equivalent text) provide translator-facing representations - Behavior control: `canCopy`, `canDelete`, `canReorder` (plus `order` on ``), `canOverlap`, `copyOf`, `isolated`, `type` (e.g., `fmt`, `ui`) - Defines a URI fragment scheme (`#f=...`) for referencing inline fragments (used by QA, notes, tooling) - XLIFF 2.1 added the Translation Candidate (`mtc`) module [10] Practical crossover: Android `strings.xml` embeds `` tags (XLIFF 1.2 vocabulary) to mark non-translatable parts of strings. ## 2. Placeholder/variable protection in CAT tools - Format filters/parsers convert native markup — HTML/XML tags, printf (`%s`, `%1$s`), .NET (`{0}`), Java/ICU (`{name}`), Apple (`%@`), `${var}`, `%var%` — into **atomic inline tokens** *before* segmentation, so tokens are never split and translators cannot edit inside them. - Typical protections: locked tags; insertion via shortcut/drag; open/close pairing enforcement; auto-propagation between segments; display modes (full/partial/no native text; numbered `{1}{2}` vs. native representation). - QA/verification: missing tags, extra tags, reordered tags, empty tags — e.g., Trados Studio tag verification, memoQ QA (incl. regex-based tag definitions), OmegaT tag validation, Phrase (Memsource) tag QA, Crowdin/Lokalise variable highlighting and custom placeholder regexes. - **Pseudo-localization** (string expansion, accented characters, variable delimiting) is the standard test that placeholders survive translation intact. ## 3. ICU MessageFormat - **MF1** syntax `{arg, type, style}` [4]: types `number`, `date`, `time`, `spellout`, `ordinal`, `duration`, legacy `choice`; apostrophe-based quoting; numbered and named arguments. - **Plural/Select** [4][6]: `{count, plural, offset:1 =0{…} one{…} other{…}}` using CLDR cardinal categories (`zero, one, two, few, many, other`) and `=N` exact matches; `select` for gender/enum; `selectOrdinal`; `#` outputs the formatted number. Used in Java/ICU4J, PHP intl, FormatJS/react-intl, i18next-icu, Angular, Flutter ARB files. - **MessageFormat 2 (MF2)** [5]: redesigned spec from the Unicode message-format-wg; tech preview in ICU 75 (2024), stable in ICU 76 (Oct 2024). Adds declarations (`.input`, `.local`), selection via `.match … * {{…}}`, function placeholders (`{$count :number style=integer}`), backslash escaping, defined error/fallback behavior, a data model for tooling, and **first-class markup parts** (open/close placeholders) so inline tags can be represented without breaking message syntax. ## 4. W3C Internationalization Tag Set (ITS) - **ITS 1.0 (W3C Rec, Apr 2007)** [7]: six data categories — Translate, Localization Note, Terminology, Directionality, Language Information, Elements Within Text. Two mechanisms: global rules (`its:rules` with XPath `selector`) and local attributes. - **ITS 2.0 (W3C Rec, Oct 2013)** [8]: retains the six and adds ten — Domain, Text Analysis, Locale Filter, External Resource, Target Pointer, Id Value, Preserve Space, Localization Quality Issue, Localization Quality Rating, Provenance (16 total). Adds NIF mapping, an "ITS Tool" conformance class, and HTML5 support (native `translate`/`dir` attributes, `its-*` local attributes, external rules via ``). - Practical effect: lets tools declaratively identify translatable vs. protected content (e.g., `translate="no"`, script blocks, terminology), and its quality/provenance categories were designed for interoperability with XLIFF 2.0 workflows. ## How the pieces fit together ITS marks up what must be translated/protected upstream → the format parser (CAT tool) converts native markup into protected inline codes → XLIFF carries those codes losslessly between systems → ICU MessageFormat governs runtime substitution of variables/plurals in the localized strings. ## References [1] OASIS XLIFF 1.2, Feb 2008 — https://docs.oasis-open.org/xliff/v1.2/os/xliff-core.html [2] OASIS XLIFF 2.0, Aug 2014 — https://docs.oasis-open.org/xliff/xliff-core/v2.0/os/xliff-core-v2.0-os.html [3] OASIS XLIFF 2.2, 2020 — https://docs.oasis-open.org/xliff/xliff-core/v2.2/os/xliff-core-v2.2-os.html [4] ICU User Guide: MessageFormat — https://unicode-org.github.io/icu/userguide/format_parse/messages/ [5] MessageFormat 2.0 specification (unicode-org/message-format-wg) — https://unicode.github.io/message-format-wg/ ; ICU 76 release notes — https://icu.unicode.org/download/76 [6] UTS #35 (CLDR), Plural Rules — https://unicode.org/reports/tr35/tr35-numbers.html [7] W3C ITS 1.0 Recommendation — https://www.w3.org/TR/its/ [8] W3C ITS 2.0 Recommendation — https://www.w3.org/TR/its20/ [9] W3C Note, "Strings on the Web: Language Identifier and Direction Metadata" — https://www.w3.org/TR/string-meta/ [10] OASIS XLIFF 2.1, 2019 — https://docs.oasis-open.org/xliff/xliff-core/v2.1/os/xliff-core-v2.1-os.html --- ## Locale conventions for numbers, dates, and currencies in translation: Unicode CLDR data, plural rules, and pseudo-localization testing for format breakage # Locale Conventions in Translation: CLDR, Plural Rules & Pseudo-Localization ## 1. Unicode CLDR: the canonical locale-data source - **CLDR** (Common Locale Data Repository) is the Unicode Consortium's standard repository of locale data — the source of truth used by ICU, Chrome, Android, Windows, macOS/iOS, Java, .NET, and most i18n libraries. It covers 1,100+ locales with tiered coverage (modern / moderate / basic) and ships roughly twice a year [1]. - Data is expressed in **LDML (UTS #35)**, which defines number patterns, currency metadata, date/time patterns, calendars, plural rules, units, collation, and supplemental data (currency fractions, week data, measurement preferences, likely subtags for locale fallback) [2]. - Locale IDs support BCP 47 with Unicode extensions that override defaults: `-u-nu-arab` (numbering system), `-u-ca-islamic` (calendar), `-u-hc-h12` (hour cycle), `-u-fw-mon` (first day of week) [2]. ## 2. Number & currency conventions that vary by locale - **Separators:** `1,234.56` (en) vs `1.234,56` (de) vs `1 234,56` (fr, narrow no-break space U+202F) vs Arabic-Indic `١٬٢٣٤٫٥٦`. Grouping size is not always 3 — Indian locales use 2-2-3 grouping (`1,23,45,678`); some locales (es, it, pt) set `minimumGroupingDigits=2` so 4-digit numbers stay ungrouped [2][3]. - **Digits:** ~80 numbering systems in CLDR — Latin, Arabic-Indic, Eastern Arabic-Indic (Persian), Devanagari, Thai, plus non-positional (Roman, Hebrew) [2][3]. - **Percent placement:** `50%` (en) vs `50 %` (fr) vs `%50` (tr) [2][3]. - **Currency:** symbol position varies (`$1,234.56` / `1.234,56 €` / `1 234,56 $` in fr-CA); minor-unit digits differ (JPY = 0, BHD/KWD = 3, most = 2) via CLDR supplemental currency data; symbols are ambiguous (`$`, `£`, `kr`) so CLDR defines symbol/narrow-symbol/code/name display tiers with fallback (USD renders `$` in en-US but `US$` in en-CA) [2][3]. Cash rounding increments (e.g., CHF 0.05) also live in CLDR. ## 3. Date/time conventions - CLDR defines **full/long/medium/short** patterns plus **skeletons** (`yMMMMd`, `Ed`) that let components adapt; field *order* and separators vary (`MMMM d, y` en-US; `d. MMMM y` de; `y年M月d日` ja) — never hardcode order or slice formatted strings [2][4]. - **Calendars:** Gregorian plus Buddhist (th), Islamic, Persian (fa), Hebrew, Japanese imperial eras, Chinese lunar, Minguo (zh-TW contexts), Ethiopian, Indian national [2][4]. - **Hour cycles:** h11/h12 (12-hour + AM/PM) vs h23/h24; some locales use extended day periods (Bengali রাত/সকাল/দুপুর…). First day of week (Sun/Mon/Sat) and week-numbering rules (ISO 8601 vs US) vary [2][4]. - Also defined: interval formats ("Jan 5–7"), relative times ("5 minutes ago"), timezone display (exemplar cities, localized GMT offsets, metazone names) [2][4]. ## 4. Plural rules (UTS #35) - CLDR defines up to **six categories** — `zero, one, two, few, many, other` — selected by numeric rules over operands `n, i, v, w, f, t, e` (integer digits, fraction digits, exponent) [2][3]. - Coverage varies radically: Japanese/Chinese/Korean/Thai/Vietnamese use only `other`; English uses `one/other`; **Russian** uses `one/few/many/other` (1, 21… vs 2–4, 22–24… vs 0, 5–20…); **Arabic and Welsh use all six**; Irish uses five; **French has a `many`** category for large round numbers ("un million **d'**habitants") [2][3]. - Ordinal rules are separate (English 1st/2nd/3rd/4th → one/two/few/other); **plural ranges** ("1–3 days") have their own data [3]. - Implication: translators must supply *every* category variant, and code must use ICU `PluralRules`/MessageFormat — never `n == 1 ? "item" : "items"`. GNU gettext encodes the same logic as per-language `Plural-Forms` expressions (`nplurals=3` for Russian) [10]. ## 5. Pseudo-localization testing Pseudo-locales machine-transform source strings to expose breakage **before** real translations exist: - **Accented pseudo** (e.g., `en-XA`): maps ASCII to accented/exotic characters — reveals encoding bugs, missing glyphs, hardcoded strings [7][8]. - **Expansion pseudo:** pads strings (~30–40% longer, matching German/French growth) wrapped in delimiters (`[!!! Hëllô !!!]`) — reveals truncation, overflow, and **concatenation bugs** (brackets appearing mid-sentence) [7][8][9]. - **Pseudo-bidi** (e.g., `ar-XB`): substitutes RTL-looking characters and inserts directional marks — surfaces bidi/layout/mirroring bugs [7][8]. - **Format-breakage detection:** pseudo runs verify placeholder integrity (`{0}`, `%s`, `{{name}}`), that ICU patterns survive, and that no code assumes `"."` decimals or `MM/DD/YYYY`. Xcode previews ship Double-Length, Accented, and Right-to-Left pseudolanguages; Android exposes en-XA/ar-XB in developer options [7][9]. - **Limits:** pseudo-locales still use English plural rules and don't test real Arabic shaping or Russian plural categories — complement with snapshot tests against real locales (de-DE, ar-EG, ru-RU, ja-JP, hi-IN). ## 6. Common format-breakage failure modes - `Date.parse("01/02/2025")` — ambiguous, locale-dependent parsing; store ISO 8601 / epoch, format only at display time. - `toFixed(2).replace(".", ",")` — breaks grouping, negatives, currencies. - Hardcoded `$` or assumed 2 decimals (breaks JPY, BHD). - Locale-blind `toUpperCase()` (Turkish dotless-ı problem). - Concatenated sentence fragments (word order differs per language; grammatical gender needs `select`). - Missing ICU MessageFormat: `{count, plural, one {# book} other {# books}}`. ## 7. Tooling stack ICU (C/Java/Rust-ICU4X) is the reference implementation [5]; ECMAScript `Intl.*` (`NumberFormat`, `DateTimeFormat`, `PluralRules`, `ListFormat`, `RelativeTimeFormat`) is CLDR-backed [6]; JDK 9+ defaults to CLDR data; .NET 5+ and Windows 10 1903+ use ICU. **Unicode MessageFormat 2.0** (finalized 2024) modernizes the message syntax [2][5]. --- **Sources** [1] Unicode CLDR project & release notes — cldr.unicode.org [2] UTS #35: Unicode Locale Data Markup Language (LDML) — unicode.org/reports/tr35 [3] UTS #35 Part 3: Numbers (tr35-numbers) — number patterns, currency data, plural rules [4] UTS #35 Part 4: Dates (tr35-dates) — calendars, patterns, time zones [5] ICU (International Components for Unicode) documentation — unicode-org/icu [6] ECMA-402: ECMAScript Internationalization API spec [7] Android Developers: Test with pseudo-locales (en-XA, ar-XB) [8] Chromium L10n guides: pseudo locales [9] Apple Developer: Xcode preview pseudolocalization options [10] GNU gettext manual: Plural-Forms / nplurals --- ## Localization quality assurance workflows: automated QA checks for tag mismatch and number mismatch, LQA review, and regression testing of localized builds # Localization QA Workflows: Research Summary ## Search Execution Queries run: localization QA automated checks tag/number mismatch; Xbench/Verifika QA checker capabilities; LQA review process MQM DQF scoring; localization regression testing localized builds; pseudo-localization testing. --- ## 1. Automated QA Checks (Tag Mismatch, Number Mismatch) Automated QA (also called "QA checks" or "translation QA") runs on bilingual files or TMS segments before human review, flagging mechanical errors introduced during translation or file manipulation: - **Tag/formatting mismatch**: Detects missing, extra, duplicated, or reordered inline tags (e.g., ``, `{0}`, `%s`, ``) between source and target. Tag errors are among the most common causes of broken localized UIs and runtime crashes, since tags often map to formatting, variables, or markup [1][2][3]. - **Number mismatch**: Compares numeric values in source vs. target to catch dropped, altered, or mistranslated figures (prices, quantities, dates, version numbers). Advanced checkers normalize for locale conventions (decimal comma vs. point, digit grouping) to reduce false positives [2][4]. - **Additional standard checks**: untranslated segments, source=target (untranslated copy-paste), terminology/glossary violations, inconsistency across segments, forbidden characters, double spaces, leading/trailing whitespace, capitalization, punctuation mismatch, URL/email integrity, and length limits (critical for UI strings) [1][2][3]. **Common tools**: XBench (de-facto industry standard, free), SDL Trados Studio QA Checker, memoQ QA, Verifika, QA Distiller, plus built-in QA in cloud TMS platforms (Phrase, Smartling, Crowdin, Lokalise, Transifex). Most support custom QA profiles, ignore-lists, and batch mode across multiple files/languages [1][3][5]. **Workflow position**: QA checks run (a) continuously as translators type in CAT tools, (b) as a gate before delivery to reviewers, and (c) as a final pre-release batch check. Errors are triaged as real vs. false positive, fixed, and re-run until zero critical errors remain [2][3]. --- ## 2. LQA (Language Quality Assurance) Review LQA is the human evaluation layer, typically performed by a second linguist or reviewer: - **Frameworks**: The industry has converged on **MQM (Multidimensional Quality Metrics)** — with error categories such as Accuracy, Fluency, Terminology, Style, Locale Convention, and Design/Format — and TAUS **DQF**. The older LISA QA Model is deprecated but its scoring concepts persist [6][7][8]. - **Scoring**: Reviewers annotate errors with type and severity (minor/major/critical), apply weighted point deductions, and compute a quality score (e.g., pass thresholds commonly around 95–99 points out of 100). Critical errors (e.g., mistranslation of safety content, broken tag causing data loss) may trigger automatic failure regardless of total score [7][8]. - **Sampling**: Full review is expensive, so LQA often uses sampling (e.g., a percentage of segments or fixed word counts per deliverable), with 100% review reserved for high-risk content (legal, medical, UI strings shipped to millions of users) [7][9]. - **Feedback loop**: LQA results feed back to translators for correction and to vendors for scorecards; recurring error patterns drive training, glossary/style-guide updates, and machine translation post-editing rules [6][8]. - **Trend**: Automated LQA tools and LLM-based quality estimation (QE) increasingly supplement human review, producing MQM-aligned annotations at scale; human LQA is then focused on disputed or high-stakes samples [8][9]. --- ## 3. Regression Testing of Localized Builds Localization/regression testing verifies that localized software builds actually work — complementing the text-level QA above: - **Pseudo-localization**: Before real translations exist, strings are machine-transformed (accented characters, string expansion ~30–40%, bracket delimiters, concatenated hard-coded strings exposed) to catch hard-coding, truncation, encoding, and layout issues early — cheap to automate in CI [10][11][12]. - **Internationalization (i18n) testing**: Verifies locale handling — date/number/currency formats, sorting/collation, RTL layout mirroring, Unicode handling, input methods [11][12]. - **Localized build regression**: After translations are integrated, smoke tests and regression suites run against each language build to verify: UI strings fit their containers (no truncation/overlap), variables/placeholders render correctly at runtime, hotkeys/accelerators don't collide in translated labels, and localized resources load without missing-key errors [10][12][13]. - **Automation approaches**: Screenshot/visual comparison per locale, automated UI test frameworks (Selenium, Appium, Playwright) parameterized by locale, string-length assertions, and checking that no untranslated English "leaks" into localized UIs. Crowdin, Lokalise, and Phrase offer in-context preview and screenshot tools that tie strings to UI for verification [5][12][13]. - **CI/CD integration**: Best practice is gating builds — automated QA checks on files (Section 1) run at commit/merge, pseudo-localization runs in CI, and localized smoke suites run per release candidate; failures route back to either engineering (tag/layout bugs) or localization team (translation bugs) [10][12]. --- ## 4. Typical End-to-End Workflow 1. **Pre-flight**: string freeze → pseudo-localization + i18n testing [10][11] 2. **Translation**: CAT/TMS with real-time QA checks (tags, numbers, terminology) [1][2] 3. **Automated QA gate**: batch QA run (XBench/TMS) — all critical errors resolved [1][3] 4. **LQA review**: human review per MQM/DQF, sampling-based, scored, feedback loop [6][7][8] 5. **Build integration**: translated files compiled; automated checks for missing keys/tags in resource files [12][13] 6. **Localized regression**: smoke + regression suites per language, visual/length checks, in-context review [10][12][13] 7. **Release + monitoring**: user-reported issues feed back into glossary, QA profiles, and test cases [8][12] --- ## Sources [1] XBench — QA checks documentation (translation quality checks: tag integrity, number consistency, terminology, inconsistency) [2] Phrase (Memsource) Documentation — "QA checks" and "Translation Quality" (tag mismatch, number mismatch, check profiles) [3] SDL/RWS Trados Studio Documentation — QA Checker / Verification settings (tags, numbers, punctuation, terminology) [4] Verifika Documentation — automatic QA checks (numbers, tags, terminology, consistency) [5] Lokalise / Crowdin Documentation — built-in QA checks and in-context preview tools [6] TAUS Dynamic Quality Framework (DQF) — error typology and scoring methodology [7] MQM (Multidimensional Quality Metrics) — qt21.eu/mqm — error hierarchy, severity weights, scoring [8] CSA Research / industry publications on LQA programs — sampling, thresholds, vendor scorecards [9] Google/Microsoft MT quality estimation research and LLM-based MQM annotation papers (2023–2025) [10] Microsoft Internationalization documentation — pseudo-localization guidance [11] W3C / W3C Internationalization articles — i18n testing practices [12] Smartling / Phrase blog & docs — localization testing, pseudo-localization, CI/CD integration [13] Selenium/Appium/Playwright documentation — locale-parameterized UI test automation *Note: Source [N] references map to the documentation and research bodies cited above; specific URLs retrieved during search are consolidated here by product/organization name.*"

Where these errors live in the MQM tree MQM exists in two main forms: the **full typology** (~100 issue types) and the **MQM 2021 revision** (simplified set used in WMT evaluation) [1][2]. | Error type | Full MQM tree | MQM 2021 revision | |---|---|---| | **Entity errors** | Accuracy → Mistranslation (wrong entity), or Locale convention → Name format / Person names (formatting of names) | Dedicated **Naming** type: "incorrect name for a person, place, or organization" | | **Number errors** (wrong values) | Accuracy → Mistranslation | Dedicated **Number** type: "numbers that do not match the source" | | **Number errors** (formatting only) | Locale convention → Number format | Locale convention | | **Markup errors** | Design → **Markup** | Design | Note: "Accuracy/Mistranslation" is a two-level structure — **Accuracy** is the top-level branch; **Mistranslation** is its leaf subtype (alongside Addition, Omission, Untranslated) [1][2]. ## 2. Background: the rare-word problem Early NMT with fixed vocabularies mapped rare tokens — proper names, numbers, markup — to ``, causing omissions and artifacts. Luong et al. (2015) documented this systematically, categorized rare-word errors (names, numbers, etc.), and showed post-hoc fixes (alignment-based UNK replacement, a copy mechanism, and a "positional all-transduce" method targeting numbers) recover up to ≈+2.8 BLEU on WMT'14 [1]. Koehn & Knowles (2017) listed rare words as one of six persistent NMT challenges, showing sharp quality degradation as rare-word density rises [17]. BPE subword models (Sennrich et al., 2016) largely solved open-vocabulary translation [3], but did not fully fix numbers (arbitrary digit grouping) or entity-level phenomena (transliteration choice, cross-sentence consistency). ## 2. Copy mechanisms and pointer-generator networks - **CopyNet** (Gu et al., 2016): end-to-end copying via "predictive copying," able to copy token segments; improves handling of rare tokens and names [4]. - **Pointer-softmax** (Gulcehre et al., 2016): hybrid generate/copy switch for NMT; gains concentrated on named entities and diminished in large-data/large-vocabulary regimes (where BPE already covers most tokens) [5]. - **Pointer-sentinel** (Merity et al., 2016/17): pointer mechanism for language modeling; canonical reference in the pointer-model lineage [6]. - **Pointer-generator** (See et al., 2017): mixes the generation softmax with an attention-derived copy distribution (plus coverage); despite being a summarization paper, this is the standard "pointer-generator network" architecture adopted by later NMT work [7]. - **Low-resource evidence**: Umugwaneza et al. (AFRICON 2023) compared an LSTM attention seq2seq baseline, CopyNet, and a pointer-generator for Kinyarwanda→English; copy-augmented models outperformed the baseline, with error analysis showing better retention of named entities, numbers, and OOV words [8]. - Known limitation: the copy/generate decision can miscalibrate — over-copying words that should be translated, or failing to copy when needed [4][5][7]. ## 3. Entity annotation / replacement methods - **Source-side annotation**: appending NER tags (with lemma/POS) as input features improved entity translation [9]. - **Placeholder masking/replacement**: detect entities with NER, replace them with type-tagged unique placeholders in training and inference, then re-insert translations. Bunk et al. (2019) applied this for English→German, reporting BLEU gains and fewer entity errors (with dictionary-based re-substitution and copy fallback) [10]. Hoang et al. (2018) used entity masking with unique identifiers during back-translation to force the model to copy entities [11]. - **Lexicons and hard constraints**: soft lexicon biasing improves rare-word/entity output [12]; lexically constrained decoding enforces required target terms [13][14]; Dinu et al. (2019) trained models to apply glossaries via placeholder-style special tokens, improving exact term usage [15]. - **Retrieval**: kNN-MT retrieves similar (source, target) pairs from a translation memory, helping rare-token and entity consistency [16]. - **Character-level modeling**: fully character-level NMT handles names without segmentation artifacts [21]. ## 4. Documented failure modes **Numbers** - Pre-BPE: numbers frequently became UNKs [1]. With subwords: digit strings are split into arbitrary fragments → dropped, duplicated, or mistranslated digits; poor generalization to unseen lengths/values; verbatim source-copying even when locale conventions differ (decimal/grouping separators, dates) [3][17][18][20]. - Language-model studies confirm digit sequences are poorly modeled without format-aware treatment [18]. - Mitigations: digit-aware/protected tokenization, copy mechanisms, placeholder protection, constrained decoding, numeric post-validation [1][4][10][13][14][15]. **Names** - Rare/unseen person and place names → UNK omission, hallucination, inconsistent transliteration, or copying when an established target-language exonym exists; strong sensitivity to character-level noise (typos, casing) [1][17][19]. - Entity errors are among the highest-severity categories in MQM-style quality evaluation [20]. - Mitigations: copy/pointer models (especially low-resource) [4][5][8]; entity masking/replacement [10][11]; lexicons/constraints [12][13][14][15]; retrieval [16]. **Inline markup (tags, placeholders)** - Models trained on plain text delete, duplicate, misorder, or misnest tags and corrupt placeholders (`%s`, `{0}`, ``); long-range reordering makes positional preservation hard.
